clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive neuropathy caused by FIG4 variants, notable for a strikingly asymmetric course and a mixed picture combining features of both demyelination and prominent axonal loss.
Age of onset is unusually variable, from early childhood to late adulthood, and the tempo can be unexpectedly rapid with subacute worsening that mimics an acquired neuropathy.
Both proximal and distal weakness can occur, sometimes with a lower-motor-neuron appearance and profound wasting, contrasting with the classic length-dependent distal pattern of most CMT.
Nerve conduction studies typically show intermediate or non-uniform slowing with reduced amplitudes, reflecting the combined demyelinating and axonal pathology.
Allelism is important: FIG4 variants also cause Yunis-Varon syndrome and contribute to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and certain leukodystrophies, so the phenotypic spectrum is broad.
The asymmetry, fluctuating tempo and subacute relapses often trigger evaluation for CIDP before the genetic cause is recognised.
There is no specific therapy; care is supportive with rehabilitation, orthotics and vigilance for treatable mimics.
reference.pathophysiology: CMT4J is caused by biallelic variants in FIG4 (also known as SAC3), which encodes a phosphoinositide 5-phosphatase that, in a complex with PIKFYVE and VAC14, regulates the cellular pool of phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate on late endosomal and lysosomal membranes. FIG4 paradoxically is required both to degrade and to sustain normal levels of this signalling lipid, and its loss leads to enlarged vacuolar structures and impaired endosomal-lysosomal trafficking and autophagy in neurons and Schwann cells. Most affected individuals are compound heterozygotes carrying a common hypomorphic missense allele together with a null allele, producing severe but variable dysfunction. The resulting disruption of membrane and vesicle homeostasis causes degeneration of large motor and sensory neurons alongside Schwann cell dysfunction, explaining the mixed demyelinating and axonal features, the asymmetry and the sometimes fulminant, subacute clinical course that distinguishes CMT4J from other CMT4 subtypes.
additionalDifferentials: CMT4C (SH3TC2) and other autosomal recessive demyelinating (CMT4) subtypes
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, given the asymmetry and subacute relapses
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and other motor neuron disorders (FIG4 is an ALS-related gene)
Multifocal motor neuropathy and other asymmetric acquired neuropathies
Intermediate CMT of other genetic causes
Yunis-Varon syndrome as part of the FIG4 allelic spectrum
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography, expecting intermediate or non-uniform slowing with reduced amplitudes and asymmetry
FIG4 sequencing including detection of the common hypomorphic allele, or a gene panel/exome
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis and inflammatory markers to help exclude CIDP when the course is subacute
Nerve or muscle imaging to characterise the distribution and asymmetry of involvement
Sural nerve biopsy if genetics are inconclusive, seeking mixed demyelinating and axonal changes
Family segregation studies given autosomal recessive, frequently compound-heterozygous, inheritance
redFlags: Subacute or rapidly progressive weakness prompting careful exclusion of a treatable acquired neuropathy such as CIDP
Marked asymmetry or bulbar and respiratory involvement raising concern about severe or life-threatening progression
Emergence of upper-motor-neuron signs suggesting an ALS-like phenotype within the FIG4 spectrum
Profound proximal weakness compromising mobility and safety
reference.prognosis: CMT4J is highly variable: some individuals have mild, slowly progressive disease while others suffer a severe, asymmetric and rapidly progressive course leading to substantial weakness and, when respiratory muscles are involved, reduced life expectancy. Outcome correlates broadly with the severity of the FIG4 allele combination.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the subacute, asymmetric presentation as CIDP and committing to prolonged ineffective immunotherapy
Expecting a symmetric length-dependent pattern and dismissing FIG4 because the distribution is atypical
Overlooking the broad FIG4 allelic spectrum, including ALS and Yunis-Varon syndrome, when counselling families
Assuming a benign slowly progressive course, as some patients deteriorate rapidly and unpredictably
references: International consensus guidance on inherited neuropathy classification
management: No disease-specific pharmacotherapy; supportive and rehabilitative care through a neuromuscular multidisciplinary team
Careful distinction from CIDP using electrophysiology, cerebrospinal fluid and imaging to avoid unnecessary immunotherapy for the subacute, asymmetric relapses
Physiotherapy, orthoses and mobility aids tailored to the variable proximal and distal weakness
Respiratory surveillance with non-invasive ventilation should respiratory muscles become involved
Neuropathic pain management with gabapentinoids or tricyclic agents
Avoidance of neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine
Autosomal recessive genetic counselling with detection of the common hypomorphic allele and family screening
